sections.title: One dry year on a bare volcanic rock
sections.intro_md:
In **1977** almost no rain fell on **Daphne Major**, a small volcanic cone in the Galápagos. The island got **24 mm** in the whole wet season. Plants stopped making small soft seeds. What was left were big, hard seeds that only a strong beak could crack.

Two British biologists, **Peter and Rosemary Grant**, had been catching, measuring and ringing nearly every finch on the island since 1973. So when most of the medium ground finches died that year, they knew exactly which ones died. The survivors had, on average, bigger and deeper beaks. Their chicks inherited those beaks. In one generation the population had measurably changed.

That is evolution, seen in real time, in a place Charles Darwin had visited 142 years earlier. It is not a slow mystery locked in the past. It is a measurable shift in which versions of genes get passed on, and it can happen in a single dry season. Today is about how that works: the four forces that change living things, the evidence from rocks, bodies and DNA, the experiments that watch it happen, and the myths that still cling to it.

spotlights.name: The 1977 Daphne Major drought
spotlights.spot_it: A bald, steep-sided tuff cone with a crater in the middle, sticking out of the Pacific.
spotlights.story_md: Daphne Major is about **0.3 square kilometres**, small enough to count every bird. Before the drought the Grants' team had measured the beaks of hundreds of **medium ground finches** (*Geospiza fortis*). After the 1977 drought only a small fraction were left alive, and they were not a random sample. Birds with beaks only about half a millimetre deeper could crack the woody fruit of *Tribulus* and survive. Their offspring, measured the next year, had deeper beaks too. A difference you could barely see with the naked eye decided who lived.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first time natural selection was measured in a wild vertebrate as it happened, generation by generation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a millimetre of beak was the difference between life and death.

spotlights.name: The Big Bird lineage
spotlights.spot_it: A ground finch noticeably bigger than its neighbours, with a heavier beak and an odd song.
spotlights.story_md: In **1981** a single male finch flew in that did not fit. He was more than **5 grams heavier** than the local ground finches. The Grants called his line **Big Bird**. A 2015 genome study traced him to the cactus finch of **Española**, about 100 km away. He mated with local medium ground finches, and his descendants sang his unusual song. Females chose males by song, so the lineage began breeding only among itself. A 2017 paper in *Science* argued that after just a couple of generations it behaved as a separate species, one of the fastest speciation events ever recorded.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a new species can start from a single immigrant and a mismatched song.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lost bird, one strange song, one new lineage.

sections.title: What evolution is, in one page
sections.intro_md:
Strip away the arguments and evolution has a plain definition: **a change in the inherited traits of a population over generations**. Biologists measure it as a change in how common particular versions of genes, called **alleles**, are.

Four forces move those numbers:

- **Mutation** makes new variation, a copying error in DNA.
- **Natural selection** keeps variants that help their owners survive and reproduce in that place, at that time.
- **Genetic drift** changes frequencies by pure chance, strongest in small populations.
- **Gene flow** mixes variants when individuals move between populations.

Sexual selection, the choosiness of mates, is a special and loud case of selection. **Speciation** is what happens when populations drift apart so far they no longer interbreed.

Individuals do not evolve. A giraffe cannot stretch its neck and pass on the stretch. Populations evolve, because some individuals leave more offspring than others. Keep that in mind through the day: almost every misunderstanding about evolution comes from forgetting it.

spotlights.name: LUCA, the last universal common ancestor
spotlights.spot_it: Not a fossil but a reconstruction: the genes every living cell still shares.
spotlights.story_md: Every living thing, from *E. coli* to a banyan tree to you, uses the same genetic code and many of the same core proteins. Trace that shared toolkit back and you reach **LUCA**, the last universal common ancestor. A **2024** study in *Nature Ecology and Evolution* estimated LUCA lived about **4.2 billion years ago**, only a few hundred million years after Earth formed, and carried about **2,600 protein-coding genes**. It may already have had a primitive defence system against viruses. LUCA was not the first life; it was the last ancestor all survivors share. Its relatives left no descendants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the root that makes the tree of life a single tree.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every cell on Earth is a cousin of every other.

sections.title: Two men, one idea, twenty years apart
sections.intro_md:
The idea that species change is older than Darwin. His own grandfather **Erasmus Darwin** wrote about it in the 1790s, and in **1809** the French naturalist **Jean-Baptiste Lamarck** published a full theory in which creatures improved by use and passed the gains on. What nobody had was a mechanism that worked without a guiding hand.

Darwin found one between **1837 and 1838**, after the voyage of HMS *Beagle* and after reading **Thomas Malthus** on how populations outrun their food. If more are born than can survive, any heritable edge will spread. Then he sat on the idea for **about 20 years**, breeding pigeons, dissecting barnacles for eight years, and gathering evidence.

In June **1858** a letter arrived from **Alfred Russel Wallace**, a collector working in the Malay Archipelago. It described the same mechanism. Friends arranged for both men's papers to be read at the Linnean Society of London on **1 July 1858**. Neither man was in the room. Darwin rushed out his "abstract", which became *On the Origin of Species*, in November 1859.

spotlights.name: HMS Beagle and the five-year voyage
spotlights.spot_it: A small three-masted Royal Navy survey ship, about 27 metres long, with 74 people aboard.
spotlights.story_md: Darwin was **22** and meant to become a clergyman when he joined the *Beagle* as a gentleman companion to Captain Robert FitzRoy. The voyage was planned for two years and lasted almost **five**. Darwin spent most of it on land: in Brazil's forests, the Argentine pampas where he dug up giant extinct ground sloths, and the Andes, where he found seashells high in the mountains. He was horribly seasick throughout. The **Galápagos** stop in 1835 lasted only about **five weeks**. He collected finches there but labelled them carelessly, and only later realised how much they mattered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The fossils, islands and earthquakes he saw made a fixed, unchanging world impossible for him to believe in.
spotlights.memory_hook: A seasick 22-year-old, a five-year detour, and the biggest idea in biology.

spotlights.name: The 'I think' tree, Notebook B
spotlights.spot_it: A rough ink sketch of branching lines, labelled A, B, C, D, under the words 'I think'.
spotlights.story_md: In a private notebook in **1837**, a year after he got home, Darwin drew a small tree. A single root at '1' splits into branches; some end in dead stubs, others reach the tips marked A to D. Above it he wrote two words: **'I think'**. It is the first known sketch of evolution as branching descent, where species share ancestors rather than climbing a ladder. The notebook went missing from Cambridge University Library around 2000 and was presumed stolen. It was returned anonymously in a pink gift bag in **2022**, with a note wishing the librarian a happy Easter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: This tiny drawing is the template for every family tree of life drawn since.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two words and a doodle: 'I think'.

spotlights.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, bearded Victorian with round spectacles, often photographed in old age.
spotlights.story_md: Wallace had no money and no university degree. He paid for his travels by selling specimens: over eight years in the Malay Archipelago he collected about **125,000** of them. In **February 1858**, ill with fever, he worked out natural selection and posted an essay to Darwin, the one naturalist he thought would appreciate it. Wallace was gracious about Darwin's priority for the rest of his life and even titled a book *Darwinism*. He also mapped the **Wallace Line**, the invisible boundary between Asian and Australian animals, and later became a campaigner for spiritualism and against vaccination.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without his letter, Darwin might have delayed publication for years more.
spotlights.memory_hook: The co-discoverer who mailed the idea to his rival.

spotlights.name: On the Origin of Species
spotlights.spot_it: A green cloth book of about 500 pages, with one fold-out diagram: a branching tree.
spotlights.story_md: John Murray printed **1,250 copies**, and they were taken up by booksellers on the first day. The book never uses the word 'evolution' until the sixth edition of **1872**; its very last word is 'evolved'. It barely mentions humans: one line says light will be thrown on our origin. Darwin's argument starts with something everyone in Victorian England knew, pigeon breeding, and works outward. The phrase **'survival of the fittest'** was not his. It came from Herbert Spencer, and Darwin added it in the fifth edition of **1869**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned evolution from speculation into a testable scientific theory with a mechanism.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hundred pages that start with pigeons and end with 'evolved'.

spotlights.name: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly French scientist in a high collar, often shown as the loser of the story.
spotlights.story_md: Lamarck coined the word **biology** and was one of the first to argue clearly that species change over time. His mechanism was the inheritance of acquired characteristics: use strengthens an organ, disuse weakens it, and the change passes to offspring. The giraffe stretching for leaves is the classic example, though it is a later caricature. Experiments never supported the idea for traits like muscles or necks. Modern **epigenetics** shows some chemical marks on DNA can pass on for a generation or two, but these fade and do not build complex organs. Lamarck died poor and blind.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He asked the right question and got the mechanism wrong, which made Darwin's answer easier to see.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lamarck: the giraffe stretched. Darwin: the giraffes that could not reach, died.

compare.difference: Lamarck: change acquired during life is inherited. Darwin: existing variation is sifted; only the inherited differences matter.

sections.title: Natural selection, step by step
sections.intro_md:
Natural selection needs only three ingredients, and none of them is controversial on its own.

1. **Variation.** Individuals differ: beak depth, wing colour, how fast they run.
2. **Inheritance.** Some of those differences are passed from parent to offspring through genes.
3. **Differential success.** In a given environment, some variants survive and reproduce more than others.

If all three hold, the next generation will contain more of the successful variants. Nothing is planned, nothing is trying. A predator or a drought simply removes some versions more than others. Over many generations the small shifts add up.

Two words in that recipe are often skipped. **Environment**: a trait is only 'fit' somewhere. A black moth is fit on sooty bark and a liability on pale lichen. **Reproduce**: survival matters only because it leads to offspring. A long-lived animal with no young has zero fitness in the evolutionary sense. The two spotlights below follow the textbook case from the field to the gene. It has been tested and retested for decades.

spotlights.name: The peppered moth
spotlights.spot_it: A pale moth speckled like salt and pepper, and its sooty all-black twin.
spotlights.story_md: In **1848** a collector in Manchester caught an all-black *Biston betularia*. By **1895**, about **98%** of the peppered moths around Manchester were black. Coal smoke had killed the pale lichens and blackened tree bark, so pale moths stood out to birds while black ones vanished. In the **1950s** Bernard Kettlewell released marked moths and found birds ate the conspicuous form more often. After clean air laws, the trend reversed: black moths have declined steadily since about **1962** and are now rare in much of Britain. Critics later attacked Kettlewell's methods, so Michael Majerus re-ran the experiment with **4,864 moths** from 2001 to 2007. Birds still ate more of the mismatched form.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is selection in both directions, tracked over 150 years, and it survived a hostile re-examination.
spotlights.memory_hook: Soot painted the trees and birds painted the moths.

spotlights.name: The jumping gene behind the black moth
spotlights.spot_it: Not visible on the wing: a 22,000-letter stretch of DNA inserted into a gene called cortex.
spotlights.story_md: For 150 years nobody knew what made the moth black. In **2016** a team led by Ilik Saccheri found it: a **transposable element**, a piece of 'jumping' DNA about **21,925 letters** long, had landed inside a gene called *cortex*, which helps control wing scale development. By comparing how much surrounding DNA still travelled with the insertion, they estimated the mutation first appeared around **1819**, a generation before the first black moth was caught, and just as Britain's industrial smoke was thickening. The same gene region controls wing patterns in many butterflies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links the classic field story to a single, datable mutation.
spotlights.memory_hook: One jumping gene, around 1819, turned a moth black.

sections.title: What breeders proved before biologists did
sections.intro_md:
Darwin opened *On the Origin of Species* not with finches but with **domestic pigeons**, because his readers already knew the evidence. Farmers and fanciers had been running evolution experiments for thousands of years without calling them that.

**Artificial selection** works exactly like natural selection, except a human decides who breeds. Choose the heaviest grain, the tamest wolf or the pigeon with the oddest tail, breed from those, and repeat. The results are the clearest proof that selection on ordinary variation can build huge differences quickly.

Every dog breed, from a 2 kg chihuahua to a 70 kg mastiff, is still one species descended from wolves in the last 15,000 years or more. Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts are all one wild plant. Maize looks nothing like its grassy ancestor. The difference between breeding and nature is only who does the choosing, and how fast. These four cases are the ones Darwin, and every biology teacher since, reaches for first.

spotlights.name: Darwin's fancy pigeons
spotlights.spot_it: Birds that look like different species: fantails with 30 or more tail feathers, pouters with balloon chests, owls with tiny beaks.
spotlights.story_md: In **1855** Darwin built a pigeon loft at Down House and joined two London pigeon clubs, mixing with working-class breeders he called gin-drinkers. He kept nearly every breed he could buy, killed and measured them, and boiled the skeletons. His conclusion: fantails, pouters, tumblers, runts and carriers differed so much in skulls and feathers that a naturalist finding them wild would call them separate species, even separate genera. Yet all descended from the **rock dove**, *Columba livia*. A 2013 genome study confirmed it, and found the crest on many breeds comes from a single mutation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If humans could make this much difference in a few centuries, nature had millions of years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Darwin's best evidence lived in a shed in his garden.

spotlights.name: One wild cabbage, six vegetables
spotlights.spot_it: A scruffy coastal plant with grey-green leaves and yellow flowers, ancestor of the Indian bazaar's cabbage and phool gobhi.
spotlights.story_md: *Brassica oleracea* grows wild on chalk cliffs in western Europe. Breeders chose different parts to exaggerate. Select for a big tight leaf bud and you get **cabbage**. For leaves: **kale** and collards. For a swollen stem: **kohlrabi**. For side buds: **Brussels sprouts**. For flower clusters: **broccoli**, and from broccoli's arrested flower heads, **cauliflower** and the fractal **romanesco**. They can still interbreed, so they are still one species. India grows about 9 million tonnes of cauliflower and about 9 million tonnes of cabbage a year, among the largest crops of each in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how selecting on one organ at a time produces very different shapes from the same genes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your sabzi basket holds one species wearing six costumes.

spotlights.name: Teosinte to maize
spotlights.when: About 9,000 years ago, Balsas valley, Mexico
spotlights.spot_it: A wild grass with a tiny ear of 5 to 12 hard-cased kernels, next to a fat corn cob of hundreds.
spotlights.story_md: For decades botanists could not see how maize, with its huge cob, came from any wild plant. The answer is **teosinte**, a grass from southern Mexico whose ear is a thin zigzag of about a dozen kernels, each locked in a stone-hard case. Genetic work traced maize to a single domestication from Balsas teosinte about **9,000 years ago**. A handful of genes do much of the work; one, *tga1*, freed the kernel from its hard case. Farmers selecting the easiest ears to eat, season after season, built the modern cob. Maize is now one of India's three biggest grains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a step-by-step record of how a few genes and human choice transformed a plant.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a dozen stones on a stalk to a cob of 500 kernels.

spotlights.name: Belyaev's silver foxes
spotlights.spot_it: A fox that wags its tail, has floppy ears and a white-spotted coat, and licks a researcher's face.
spotlights.story_md: In **1959** the Soviet geneticist **Dmitry Belyaev**, working when genetics was still politically dangerous in the USSR, began breeding farm silver foxes for one trait only: tameness. Each generation, only the calmest few per cent bred. Within about **10 generations**, some foxes whined for attention and wagged their tails like dogs. More surprising were the side effects nobody selected for: floppy ears, curly tails, piebald coats and shorter snouts, the same package seen in dogs, pigs and cattle. His colleague **Lyudmila Trut** has run the experiment for more than 60 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It suggests selecting for behaviour alone can drag a whole bundle of physical traits along with it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Breed for friendliness and the ears flop by themselves.

sections.title: Where the variation comes from
sections.intro_md:
Darwin's great gap was heredity. He did not know how traits passed on, and the popular idea of the time, that parents' qualities blend like paint, was a problem: blending would dilute any useful new trait to nothing within a few generations.

The answer was sitting in a monastery garden in Brno. **Gregor Mendel** showed in **1866** that traits come in discrete units that do not blend. Nobody noticed until **1900**. By the **1930s and 1940s**, mathematicians and naturalists, among them **Ronald Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane, Sewall Wright, Theodosius Dobzhansky** and **Ernst Mayr**, had welded Mendel's genetics to Darwin's selection in the **modern synthesis**. In **1953** DNA's structure showed the physical basis: a four-letter code that is copied, and occasionally miscopied.

Those miscopies are **mutations**. Each human child carries about **60 to 70** brand-new ones not present in either parent. Most do nothing. A few are harmful. A very few help. The crucial point, proven in a 1943 experiment, is that mutations arise at random with respect to need. The environment does not order up the mutation it wants; it only filters what turns up.

spotlights.name: Gregor Mendel and his peas
spotlights.spot_it: A plump friar with round glasses, holding a flower; a small walled garden in Brno, Czech Republic.
spotlights.story_md: Mendel was an Augustinian friar who had failed his teaching exam in natural history. Over about eight years he grew and counted roughly **28,000 pea plants**, tracking seven traits such as seed colour and pod shape. Crossing yellow with green peas gave all yellow; the next generation split close to **3 to 1**. The green had not blended away; it had hidden. He read his results to a local society in **1865**, published in **1866**, and was ignored. He became abbot, fought a tax dispute, and died in **1884**. Three botanists rediscovered his work in **1900**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His discrete units of inheritance, later called genes, solved the problem that worried Darwin most.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three yellow to one green, and nobody listened for 34 years.

spotlights.name: The Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of bacterial cultures where resistant colonies appear in wildly uneven numbers, a few plates with hundreds, most with none.
spotlights.story_md: Do bacteria develop resistance *because* they meet a virus, or do resistant mutants already exist? **Salvador Luria** got the idea in **1943** watching a colleague win a jackpot on a slot machine at a faculty dance: wins come in rare, random bursts. If mutations were induced by the virus, every culture should have a similar number of resistant cells. If they arose randomly beforehand, a mutation early in one culture would leave a 'jackpot' of resistant descendants. He and **Max Delbrück** found jackpots. Mutations come first; selection comes later. They shared the **1969 Nobel Prize**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that mutation is random with respect to need, which is the core of Darwinian evolution.
spotlights.memory_hook: A slot machine taught biology that mutations do not take orders.

spotlights.name: Sickle cell: a trade-off written in blood
spotlights.when: HbS mutation arose several thousand years ago
spotlights.spot_it: Red blood cells bent into crescents and sickles instead of smooth discs.
spotlights.story_md: One letter change in the haemoglobin gene makes the **sickle** variant. Two copies cause sickle cell disease, painful and often fatal without care. One copy gives strong protection against severe **malaria**. So where malaria was common, in parts of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and central India, the variant was kept by selection despite its cost. **India** carries one of the largest burdens in the world, concentrated among Adivasi communities in states such as Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Gujarat. In **July 2023** India launched a national mission to screen about **7 crore people** under 40 and eliminate the disease as a public health problem by **2047**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that selection does not make perfect bodies; it makes trade-offs that suit a local environment.
spotlights.memory_hook: One copy shields you from malaria; two copies harm you.

spotlights.name: J. B. S. Haldane, Indian citizen
spotlights.spot_it: A large bald Englishman in a kurta and dhoti, barefoot, with a moustache.
spotlights.story_md: Haldane was one of the three founders of the mathematics of evolution. He calculated how fast selection could change the peppered moth, and in **1949** he suggested that inherited blood disorders persist because they protect against **malaria**, an idea confirmed for sickle cell soon after. In **1957**, angry at British policy over Suez, he moved to **Kolkata** to join the Indian Statistical Institute, wore Indian clothes, became vegetarian and took Indian citizenship in **1961**. He died in **Bhubaneswar** in 1964 and donated his body to a medical college in Kakinada. The quip that God has 'an inordinate fondness for beetles' is attributed to him, but no reliable written source has been found.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A founder of evolutionary theory chose to build his last decade of science in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Englishman who did evolution maths in a dhoti in Kolkata.

sections.title: Chance: evolution without a reason
sections.intro_md:
Not every change is adaptive. In every generation, which individuals happen to breed, and which of their two gene copies happen to pass on, is partly luck. That random sampling is **genetic drift**. In a population of millions it barely matters. In a population of fifty, it can erase a variant or make a rare one common within a few generations, regardless of whether it helps.

Two special cases make drift dramatic. A **bottleneck** happens when a population crashes, from hunting, disease or disaster, and the few survivors carry only a sample of the old variety. A **founder effect** happens when a small group starts a new population, carrying whatever variants they happened to have.

In **1968** the Japanese geneticist **Motoo Kimura** argued that most changes in DNA over evolutionary time are not shaped by selection at all but are neutral, drifting to fixation by chance. His **neutral theory** caused a fierce debate. Today most biologists accept that much of the genome changes this way, while the visible features of bodies are largely shaped by selection. Neutral changes tick at a steady rate, which is why DNA can be used as a molecular clock.

spotlights.name: Pingelap, the island of the colour-blind
spotlights.spot_it: A ring-shaped coral atoll in Micronesia, where many people squint in bright sun.
spotlights.story_md: Around **1775** a typhoon and the famine that followed left only about **20 survivors** on Pingelap atoll. One of them, the ruler, is thought to have carried a recessive gene for **achromatopsia**, total colour blindness with severe sensitivity to light. Because everyone later descended from that tiny group, the gene became common. Today something like **1 in 10** Pingelapese are fully colour-blind, against roughly 1 in 30,000 in most populations, and about a third carry the gene. The neurologist **Oliver Sacks** wrote about the island in *The Island of the Colorblind* (1996).
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest human case of a bottleneck and founder effect making a rare trait common by chance.
spotlights.memory_hook: One typhoon, twenty survivors, a whole island seeing in grey.

spotlights.name: The cheetah's genetic bottleneck
spotlights.when: Bottleneck about 10,000 or more years ago
spotlights.spot_it: A slender spotted cat with black 'tear lines' running from its eyes to its mouth.
spotlights.story_md: Cheetahs are so genetically similar that in the **1980s** researchers found unrelated cheetahs could accept **skin grafts** from one another, something normally possible only between identical twins. Their low diversity points to at least one severe population crash, probably around the end of the last ice age. Low diversity can mean poor sperm quality and vulnerability to disease. India's own Asiatic cheetahs were hunted to extinction by about 1952. In **September 2022** India flew in eight African cheetahs from Namibia to **Kuno National Park** in Madhya Pradesh, with more from South Africa in 2023. Several have died; cubs have been born in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how a past bottleneck leaves a genetic scar that still shapes a species' survival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cheetahs are so alike they can swap skin.

sections.title: Sex: the selection that builds ornaments
sections.intro_md:
Some traits make survival harder. A peacock's train is heavy, bright and slows take-off. Darwin knew such features threatened his theory, and in **1871**, in *The Descent of Man*, he proposed a second force: **sexual selection**. Traits can spread if they win mates, even if they cost their owners in other ways.

It works in two main ways. **Competition**: males (usually) fight for access to females, which favours size, weapons and armour, like stag antlers or a bull elephant seal's bulk. **Choice**: one sex, usually females, picks partners, which favours ornaments, colours, songs and dances. Ronald Fisher showed in **1930** how female preference and male ornament can feed each other in a runaway loop. Later biologists added the **handicap** idea: an ornament is believable precisely because only a healthy male can afford it.

The topic gets its own day later in this series. Here are two cases that show how strong this force can be, and one where the textbook story is still argued over.

rows.Male: Black with red and buff shoulder

spotlights.name: The Indian peacock's train
spotlights.when: Pavo cristatus; India's national bird since 1963
spotlights.spot_it: Around 200 long upper-tail feathers raised in a shimmering fan, each tipped with a blue-green eye.
spotlights.story_md: In **April 1860** Darwin wrote to the American botanist Asa Gray that looking at a peacock's feather made him feel sick, because he could not yet explain it. The train is not the tail itself but about **200** elongated upper tail coverts, up to about **1.5 metres** long, grown fresh each year and shed after the breeding season. The male raises it, turns his back, then swivels and shivers it so the feathers rattle. The colour is not pigment: tiny crystal-like structures in the barbules bend light. In India, where the peafowl is native, the dance is at its height in the monsoon, which is why poets tie it to rain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the emblem of sexual selection, a trait that only makes sense as a mate-winning advertisement.
spotlights.memory_hook: The feather that made Darwin sick.

spotlights.name: Do peahens really count eyespots?
spotlights.spot_it: Brown-grey, smaller and with no train: the bird that, in theory, does all the choosing.
spotlights.story_md: In **1991** Marion Petrie studied peafowl at Whipsnade Zoo in England and found that males with more eyespots mated more often. When she cut eyespots from some trains, those males lost mates. It became the textbook proof of female choice. Then in **2008** Mariko Takahashi's team followed a feral population in Japan for seven years and found no link between train elaborateness and mating success. Later work suggests peahens may pay more attention to how the train is shaken, the sound it makes, or the lower part of the display. The honest summary: sexual selection shaped the train, but exactly which feature females judge is still debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that famous results need replication, and that real choices are rarely about one number.
spotlights.memory_hook: Science looked twice at the peacock and got two answers.

spotlights.name: The widowbird tail-cutting experiment
spotlights.spot_it: A black bird with a red shoulder patch dragging a tail about half a metre long over the grass.
spotlights.story_md: Male long-tailed widowbirds in East and southern Africa grow tails up to about **50 cm**, several times their body length. In **1982** the Swedish biologist **Malte Andersson** caught males in Kenya and did something brutal and elegant. He cut some tails short, glued the cut pieces onto other males to make super-long tails, and left controls with a cut and re-glued tail of normal length. The super-long males attracted more nests in their territories than any other group; the shortened ones attracted fewest. It was the first experiment to show directly that female choice favours an exaggerated ornament.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a 110-year-old idea into a controlled experiment with scissors and glue.
spotlights.memory_hook: Andersson gave birds tail extensions, and females loved them.

sections.title: How one species becomes two
sections.intro_md:
A **species**, in the most common definition, is a group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring in nature. New species form when populations stop exchanging genes long enough to grow apart. The usual first step is a barrier.

- **Allopatric speciation**: a mountain, sea, river or drifting continent splits a population. Each half adapts and drifts on its own. When they meet again, they no longer mate, or their hybrids fail.
- **Sympatric speciation**: populations split while living in the same place, by switching to a new food, a new host or a new mating signal.
- **Hybrid speciation**: two species cross and the hybrids found a third line, as with the Big Bird finches.

Speciation is usually too slow to watch from start to finish, but nature leaves every stage on display at once: populations that barely differ, races that mate reluctantly, and true species that never mix. The cases below are snapshots along that road, including one where India itself was the barrier: the subcontinent's 100-million-year voyage across the ocean.

spotlights.name: The greenish warbler's ring
spotlights.spot_it: A small olive leaf-warbler with a pale wing bar, a common winter visitor to Indian forests and gardens.
spotlights.story_md: The greenish warbler breeds in a great ring around the treeless **Tibetan plateau**, with populations along the Himalaya linking those to the west and east. Moving around the ring from India, each population can interbreed with its neighbours, but songs and genes shift gradually. Where the two ends of the ring meet in **central Siberia**, the western and eastern forms live side by side and do not interbreed: their songs have become so different that the birds do not recognise each other as mates. Darren Irwin's studies showed the ring is not perfectly continuous through history, but it still lays out speciation in space.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It lets you walk through the stages of speciation on a map, starting in the Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fly round Tibet and the warblers forget each other's songs.

spotlights.name: Lake Victoria's cichlids
spotlights.spot_it: Small, brightly coloured lake fish: red-backed males here, blue males a few metres away.
spotlights.story_md: Lake Victoria seems to have **dried out almost completely** about 15,000 years ago. Since refilling, it has filled with roughly **500 species** of cichlid fish, the fastest large burst of vertebrate speciation known. They split by diet, depth and colour. In some species pairs, such as the red and blue males of *Pundamilia*, females in deeper, redder light prefer red males, and those in clearer shallow water prefer blue. Then in the **1950s** the predatory **Nile perch** was introduced for fishing. Combined with murkier, polluted water that blurred colour signals, it wiped out perhaps **200** of the species.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how mate choice and light can split species quickly, and how fast humans can undo it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hundred species in fifteen thousand years, half lost in fifty.

spotlights.name: The apple maggot fly
spotlights.when: Apple race first recorded 1864, New York
spotlights.spot_it: A small fly with banded wings that looks like it is wearing tiger stripes.
spotlights.story_md: *Rhagoletis pomonella* used to lay its eggs only in fruits of the native North American **hawthorn**. Europeans brought apple trees, and in **1864** the first maggots in apples were recorded in New York's Hudson Valley. Flies mate on the fruit they grew up in, so apple flies mostly meet apple flies. Apples ripen a few weeks earlier than hawthorn, so the apple race also emerges earlier. Within about 150 years, the two races differ genetically in timing and fruit preference, with only a few per cent gene flow between them. It is an early stage of sympatric speciation: no wall, just a new host.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows populations splitting in the same place, driven by a new food introduced by people.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fly that moved from hawthorns to apples and stopped visiting the family.

spotlights.name: The purple frog of the Western Ghats
spotlights.when: Described 2003; lineage over 60 million years old
spotlights.spot_it: A bloated purple-grey frog with a tiny pointed white snout, like a deflated balloon.
spotlights.story_md: In **2003** S. D. Biju of Delhi University and Franky Bossuyt described *Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis* from Idukki, Kerala, in *Nature*. Villagers knew it; science did not. It lives **underground** most of the year, eating termites with its pointed snout, and surfaces for about **two weeks** in the monsoon to breed in streams. DNA showed its closest living relatives are tiny frogs in the **Seychelles**, about 3,000 km away. The two lineages split when India and the Seychelles broke apart in the age of dinosaurs. India's drift north was the barrier; the frog is a passenger from Gondwana.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living record of allopatric speciation driven by continental drift, discovered in India in this century.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Gondwana relic that comes up for two weeks a year.

sections.title: The rocks keep the receipts
sections.intro_md:
Fossils are rare. Most animals rot, are eaten or crushed. Yet the record that survives is ordered in a way that only evolution explains. Simple single cells appear in rocks over **3.5 billion** years old; complex animals only in the last 600 million; fish before amphibians, amphibians before reptiles, reptiles before mammals and birds. The biologist J. B. S. Haldane is said to have answered what would disprove evolution with: fossil rabbits in the Precambrian. None have been found.

The record also contains **transitional forms**, animals with a mix of old and new features. They are not 'missing links' in a chain, a phrase scientists avoid, but side branches that show how body plans changed. Their real power is predictive. If evolution is true, an animal halfway between fish and land animals should appear in rocks of a particular age, and nowhere else. The first spotlight is what happened when a team went looking.

Below the spotlights, the timeline shows the big events in the 4.5-billion-year history of life, with years in millions.

visual.title: Life's big moments (millions of years ago, negative = past)

Great Oxidation: cyanobacteria fill the air with oxygen

spotlights.name: Tiktaalik, the fishapod
spotlights.when: Lived about 375 million years ago; found 2004
spotlights.spot_it: A flat-headed fish about 1 to 3 metres long, with a neck, scales, gills and sturdy front fins that hide wrist bones.
spotlights.story_md: Neil Shubin, Ted Daeschler and Farish Jenkins reasoned that the move from water to land happened between about **385 and 365 million years ago**. They searched geology maps for exposed river rocks of that age and found them on **Ellesmere Island** in the Canadian Arctic. After four field seasons, in **2004**, they found it. *Tiktaalik* had gills and scales like a fish, but a flat crocodile-like head, a **neck** that could move, ribs to support its body, and fins with bones matching a shoulder, elbow and wrist. The name, from Inuktitut, means a large freshwater fish. Shubin's 2008 book *Your Inner Fish* traced human anatomy back to it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was a prediction of evolution, tested by digging in the right place, and it came true.
spotlights.memory_hook: They predicted the rock, went to the Arctic, and found the fish with a neck.

spotlights.name: Archaeopteryx
spotlights.when: Lived about 150 million years ago; first skeleton 1861
spotlights.spot_it: A crow-sized skeleton pressed flat in pale limestone, with feathered wings, toothed jaws and a long bony tail.
spotlights.story_md: Just **two years** after *On the Origin of Species*, quarrymen in the fine limestone of **Solnhofen**, Bavaria, found a skeleton with the feathers of a bird and the teeth, clawed fingers and long tail of a small dinosaur. The British Museum bought it in **1862**. The more complete Berlin specimen, with its head, followed in the 1870s. Darwin's supporter Thomas Huxley used it to argue that birds came from reptiles. Today about a dozen specimens are known, and thousands of feathered dinosaur fossils from China since the 1990s make the link between dinosaurs and birds one of the best documented in the record.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A half-bird, half-dinosaur appeared at the moment Darwin's critics demanded one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Feathers on a dinosaur, delivered two years after the book.

spotlights.name: Lucy
spotlights.when: Lived about 3.2 million years ago; found 24 November 1974
spotlights.spot_it: A small partial skeleton, about 1.1 metres tall, laid out bone by bone, with a hip built for walking upright.
spotlights.story_md: Donald Johanson and Tom Gray spotted an arm bone in a gully at **Hadar, Ethiopia**, in 1974. They recovered about **40%** of a single skeleton of *Australopithecus afarensis*. That night the camp played the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is **Dinkinesh**, 'you are marvellous'. Her pelvis and knee show she walked upright, but her brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's. It settled an old argument: our ancestors stood up long before their brains grew. A 2016 study suggested she died falling from a tree, though not everyone agrees.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She showed walking upright came first and big brains came much later.
spotlights.memory_hook: Upright legs, ape-sized brain, Beatles song.

sections.title: Whales walked out of India
sections.intro_md:
For a century, whales were evolution's awkward case. A huge, hairless, fish-shaped mammal that breathes air, nurses its young and has finger bones in its flippers is plainly a mammal, but how did a land mammal end up in the ocean? Creationists pointed to the lack of intermediate fossils.

Then they turned up, and many of them were found in **India and Pakistan**. About **50 million years ago**, the Indian plate was closing in on Asia, and between them lay the shallow, warm **Tethys Sea**. Along its shores, in what are now Kashmir, Kutch in Gujarat and northern Pakistan, small hoofed mammals started wading, then swimming. The rocks there record the whole move: deer-sized waders, crocodile-like ambush hunters, otter-like coastal swimmers, and finally fully marine whales with useless little hind legs.

DNA tells the same story independently: whales sit inside the group of even-toed hoofed mammals, and their closest living relatives are **hippos**. Fossils and genes, gathered by different people with different methods, point at the same family tree.

visual.title: Where the walking whales were found

spotlights.name: Indohyus, the Kashmir wader
spotlights.when: About 48 million years ago; whale link shown 2007
spotlights.spot_it: A fox-sized hoofed animal with thick, heavy leg bones and a long tail, like a tiny deer that liked water.
spotlights.story_md: The Indian geologist **A. Ranga Rao** collected the first fossils in the **Kalakot** area of Jammu and Kashmir in 1970 and named the animal in 1971. Decades later, his widow gave the remaining rocks to the American palaeontologist **Hans Thewissen**. When a technician broke open a skull, Thewissen saw an ear bone with a thick, curled wall called the **involucrum**, a feature found only in whales. In **2007** in *Nature*, his team showed *Indohyus* had dense, heavy bones like a hippo's, used as ballast for wading. It was a land animal on the road to the sea, and the closest known relative of whales.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best candidate for what the land ancestors of whales looked like, and it came from India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whale ear in a fox-sized Kashmiri hoofed animal.

spotlights.name: Pakicetus and Ambulocetus
spotlights.spot_it: A wolf-like land animal with a long snout, and a three-metre beast like a furry crocodile with big feet.
spotlights.story_md: In **1981** Philip Gingerich described *Pakicetus* from 50-million-year-old river rocks in northern **Pakistan**. It looked like a long-snouted dog, lived on land and waded in streams, but its skull had the distinctive whale ear. In **1994** Thewissen described *Ambulocetus natans*, the 'walking, swimming whale', also from Pakistan. It was about **3 metres** long, with short legs, huge webbed hind feet, and eyes on top of its head. It probably lurked in shallow water like a crocodile and swam by undulating its body and paddling its feet. Its jaw shows it heard by picking up vibrations through the bone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They fill the gap between land mammals and seagoing whales, step by step.
spotlights.memory_hook: First a whale that walked like a dog, then one that hunted like a crocodile.

spotlights.name: Kutch whales and Basilosaurus's tiny legs
spotlights.spot_it: A slender sea serpent of a whale, up to about 18 metres, with hind legs no bigger than a child's arm.
spotlights.story_md: In **2000** Sunil Bajpai and Hans Thewissen described *Kutchicetus*, a small, otter-like early whale with a long tail, from the rocks of **Kutch, Gujarat**. Kutch has also given up *Remingtonocetus* and other coastal whales. Later, fully marine whales such as *Basilosaurus* and *Dorudon* swam the Tethys. Egypt's **Wadi Al-Hitan**, the Valley of Whales, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005, has hundreds of their skeletons lying in the desert. *Basilosaurus* still had hind legs about **60 cm** long, complete with knee, ankle and toes, far too small to walk on. They may have been used as claspers in mating.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Legs too small to walk show an animal that had left the land but not yet lost the evidence.
spotlights.memory_hook: An 18-metre whale with knees.

sections.title: Bodies that remember their history
sections.intro_md:
If living things were designed from scratch, you would expect clean solutions. What you actually find are improvisations: old parts bent to new uses, wiring that only makes sense if you know the ancestor, and broken genes left lying in the genome like old furniture in an attic.

These are some of the strongest evidence for evolution because they are hard to explain any other way. Your genome carries about **8%** leftovers of ancient viruses, called endogenous retroviruses, and many sit in exactly the same spots in the chimpanzee genome, as if inherited from a shared ancestor. Humans get goosebumps, which fluff up fur we no longer have. Babies grip with a reflex that once held onto a mother's fur.

Scientists call features that have lost their original function **vestigial**. That does not always mean useless: the human appendix may store gut bacteria, and whale hip bones anchor muscles used in mating. It means the structure is a reduced version of something that once did a different job. The four spotlights below are the classic exhibits.

spotlights.name: The giraffe's absurd nerve
spotlights.spot_it: A nerve that runs from the brain all the way down the neck, loops round a blood vessel near the heart, and climbs back up.
spotlights.story_md: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** controls the voice box. It leaves the brain, but instead of going directly to the larynx a few centimetres away, it travels down into the chest, loops under the aorta, and returns up the neck. In fish, the nerve's ancestor ran a short direct route past a gill artery. As necks lengthened and the heart moved down into the chest, the nerve stayed hooked under the artery and had to stretch. In a giraffe the detour is several metres long. In **2009** Richard Dawkins and a team of anatomists dissected a giraffe on television to trace it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: No engineer would route a cable this way; evolution can only modify what it already has.
spotlights.memory_hook: Metres of nerve to travel a few centimetres.

spotlights.name: Human chromosome 2: the fusion
spotlights.spot_it: Line up human chromosome 2 next to two chimp chromosomes, and their banding patterns match end to end.
spotlights.story_md: Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans have **24 pairs** of chromosomes; humans have **23**. If we share an ancestor, a pair must have been lost or merged. Scientists predicted a fusion, and in **1991** they found its scar. Human chromosome 2 has, in its middle, the repeated end-cap sequences called **telomeres** that normally sit only at chromosome tips, joined head to head. It also carries the remains of a second, switched-off **centromere**, exactly where one of the ape chromosomes would have had its own. Two ancestral chromosomes had fused into one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A specific, testable prediction from common ancestry, confirmed in the DNA sequence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Our chromosome 2 is two ape chromosomes glued end to end.

spotlights.name: The broken vitamin C gene
spotlights.when: Lost in our primate ancestors over 60 million years ago
spotlights.spot_it: Invisible on the body; visible in the genome as a gene with the same crippling damage in humans and apes.
spotlights.story_md: Most mammals make their own vitamin C. Humans cannot, which is why sailors died of **scurvy** on long voyages. We still carry the gene for the last step, **GULO**, but it is a broken copy, a pseudogene, with large missing chunks. Chimps, gorillas, orangutans and monkeys carry the same broken gene with matching damage, inherited from a common ancestor that ate enough fruit not to miss it. Guinea pigs also cannot make vitamin C, but their GULO broke independently, with different mutations. Shared mistakes in the same places are like shared typos in two copies of an essay: they reveal a common source.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shared broken genes are strong evidence of common ancestry.
spotlights.memory_hook: We share our scurvy with the apes, typo for typo.

spotlights.name: How an eye can evolve
spotlights.spot_it: A nautilus eye: an open cup with a pinhole and no lens, a living stage between a light patch and a camera eye.
spotlights.story_md: Darwin admitted it seemed absurd that an eye could form by selection, then explained how: a series of small, useful steps, each still found in living animals. Flatworms have light-sensitive patches; limpets have cups; the **nautilus** has a pinhole camera eye with no lens; squid and octopus have full lens eyes. In **1994** Dan-Eric Nilsson and Susanne Pelger modelled the steps from a flat patch to a camera eye, assuming 1% improvements at a time. Their pessimistic estimate: about **364,000 generations**, well under half a million years for a small animal. Eyes have evolved independently many times.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the classic objection to evolution into one of its best-understood examples.
spotlights.memory_hook: From freckle to camera in under half a million years.

sections.title: Evolution you can watch
sections.intro_md:
The usual objection is that nobody has ever seen evolution happen. In fact it is watched daily, in labs, hospitals and islands, wherever generations are short or pressure is extreme.

Bacteria are the perfect subject. *E. coli* can divide every 20 minutes. Freeze a sample, and you have a fossil record you can bring back to life and race against its own descendants. Viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 change so quickly that vaccines must be updated; the variant names of 2021 and 2022 were evolution reported on the evening news.

The most dangerous case is **antimicrobial resistance**. Every course of antibiotics is a selection experiment: susceptible bacteria die, resistant ones are left with the space to themselves. A 2024 study in *The Lancet* estimated that resistant bacterial infections directly caused about **1.14 million deaths** in 2021, and forecast about **39 million** such deaths between 2025 and 2050. India, with high antibiotic use and a large burden of infection, is central to this story. Its 'Red Line' campaign, launched in 2016, marks prescription-only antibiotic packs with a red vertical line.

spotlights.name: Lenski's 12 flasks
spotlights.spot_it: Twelve small glass flasks of cloudy liquid swirling in an incubator, one noticeably cloudier than the rest.
spotlights.story_md: On **24 February 1988** Richard Lenski at Michigan State University started **12 populations** of *E. coli* from a single ancestor, in a broth with a little glucose. Every day since, someone has moved 1% of each flask into fresh broth, about **6.6 generations** a day. Every 500 generations a sample is frozen, a living fossil record. The populations passed **75,000 generations** in 2022, when the experiment moved to Jeffrey Barrick's lab in Texas, and **80,000** in August **2024**. In **2025** it moved back to Michigan State with Barrick. All 12 grew fitter and bigger-celled, and they are still improving, with no plateau yet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the longest-running evolution experiment, and evolution's most direct live demonstration.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eighty thousand generations of germs, one flask change a day since 1988.

spotlights.name: The citrate eaters
spotlights.spot_it: One flask, Ara-3, suddenly turning much cloudier than the other eleven.
spotlights.story_md: The broth contained plenty of **citrate**, but *E. coli* cannot use it when oxygen is present; that inability is part of how the species is defined. Around generation **31,500**, in just one of the 12 populations, bacteria evolved to eat it, and the flask turned cloudy with their numbers. Zachary Blount replayed history from the frozen samples. Only clones from after about generation 20,000 could re-evolve the trait, because earlier, otherwise silent mutations had set the stage. Evolution depended on its own history: **historical contingency**, measured in a freezer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed a genuinely new ability evolving in the lab, and why some innovations are so rare.
spotlights.memory_hook: One flask in twelve learned to eat the furniture.

spotlights.name: The mega-plate
spotlights.spot_it: A giant rectangular Petri dish, with white bacterial fronts advancing in bands towards a black centre.
spotlights.story_md: Michael Baym and Roy Kishony's team built a dish about **60 by 120 cm** and divided it into bands. The outer bands had no antibiotic; each band inward had about **ten times** more, up to about **1,000 times** the dose that kills normal *E. coli*. Bacteria seeded at the edges spread, stalled at each new band, and then broke through as a resistant mutant appeared, branching like a tree. In about **11 days** they reached the centre. Time-lapse video turned an abstract statistic into something you can watch: resistance does not take decades to build; under steady pressure, it builds in days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made antibiotic resistance visible, step by step.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eleven days from no defence to a thousandfold dose.

spotlights.name: NDM-1, the gene that travels
spotlights.spot_it: A Petri dish where bacteria grow right up to antibiotic discs that should have cleared a ring around them.
spotlights.story_md: In **2008** a Swedish man of Indian origin, treated in hospital in **New Delhi**, came home with a *Klebsiella* infection that shrugged off carbapenems, the last-line antibiotics. The enzyme responsible was named **New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase 1** in 2009. A 2010 *Lancet Infectious Diseases* study found it in India, Pakistan and Britain. India's health ministry objected to the name, saying it unfairly tied a global problem to one city. The gene sits on **plasmids**, small DNA loops that bacteria pass to one another, even across species. That horizontal transfer is evolution by sharing, and it is why resistance spreads so fast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that bacteria do not only mutate; they trade resistance genes like files.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gene with a city's name that moves between species.

spotlights.name: The lizards of Pod Mrčaru
spotlights.spot_it: A green-backed Mediterranean lizard with a striped pattern, basking on a rock.
spotlights.story_md: In **1971** researchers moved **five pairs** of Italian wall lizards from the Croatian islet of Pod Kopište to nearby Pod Mrčaru, where the species did not live. War in Yugoslavia kept scientists away until **2004**. The lizards had taken over the island and changed their diet: they now ate mostly plants in summer instead of insects. In a **2008** paper the team reported bigger heads, a stronger bite, and something new: **cecal valves**, muscular folds in the gut that slow digestion so bacteria can break down plant matter. This structure is absent in the source population and rare in the lizard family. All of it took about 36 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A new gut structure appeared in about 30 generations after a shift in diet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five pairs of lizards, 36 years, a new valve in the gut.

spotlights.name: Gorongosa's tuskless elephants
spotlights.spot_it: Adult female African elephants with no tusks at all, common in Mozambique's Gorongosa park.
spotlights.story_md: During Mozambique's civil war, about **90%** of the elephants in **Gorongosa National Park** were killed, many for ivory to fund the fighting. Poachers left tuskless elephants alone. Before the war about **18.5%** of females were naturally tuskless. Among females born after it, the share was about **51%**. A **2021** study in *Science* found the trait is linked to the X chromosome and appears to be **lethal in males**, which is why tuskless elephants are almost all female. Poaching acted as an extremely strong selection pressure, changing a population's anatomy within about one generation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is human-driven selection in a wild animal, measured and traced to genes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ivory hunters bred elephants without tusks.

sections.title: Humans are still evolving
sections.intro_md:
Our species is about **300,000 years** old, and it has not stopped evolving. In the last 10,000 years, farming, herding, new diets, high altitude and new diseases have all left marks in human DNA. Ancient DNA, the field that won **Svante Pääbo** the **2022 Nobel Prize**, now lets geneticists read genomes from people who lived thousands of years ago and measure the changes directly.

Some adaptations came from interbreeding. Everyone outside Africa carries roughly **1 to 2%** Neanderthal DNA, and many people in Asia and Oceania also carry DNA from the **Denisovans**, a sister group first identified in 2010 from a finger bone in a Siberian cave. Some of those borrowed genes were useful: they help with immunity, skin and high-altitude breathing.

India is a rich place to study this. Its people descend largely from mixtures of ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers, early farmers related to people of the Iranian plateau, and later groups from the steppe, mixed in different proportions. Thousands of years of marrying within communities, **endogamy**, means many Indian groups behave genetically like separate populations, which helps researchers but also concentrates some recessive diseases.

visual.title: Rough share of adults worldwide who digest lactose (%)

spotlights.name: Drinking milk as an adult
spotlights.spot_it: A grown adult drinking a glass of milk without discomfort: a mutant trait in global terms.
spotlights.story_md: All mammals make **lactase**, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, as babies, and most switch it off after weaning. About **one in three** adults worldwide still makes it, thanks to mutations that keep the gene switched on. These spread with dairying, in Europe, East Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, several times independently, by different mutations: a textbook case of convergent evolution in humans. In India, lactase persistence is generally more common in the north and west, where herding has deep roots, and less common in the south and east, but it varies widely by community.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a recent, strong selection in humans driven by a cultural change: keeping cattle.
spotlights.memory_hook: The ability to drink milk as an adult is a mutation that rode on the backs of cows.

spotlights.name: Tibetans and the Denisovan gene
spotlights.spot_it: People living above 4,000 metres who do not get thick, sludgy blood the way lowlanders do.
spotlights.story_md: At **4,000 metres**, air holds about 40% less oxygen than at sea level. Most lowlanders who move up make more red blood cells, which thickens the blood and raises the risk of stroke. Tibetans do not; they have other ways of coping. Much of the difference traces to a version of the gene **EPAS1**. In **2014** a team showed this version almost certainly came from **Denisovans**, through interbreeding tens of thousands of years ago. It stayed rare until people settled the plateau, when selection made it common. An ancient cousin's gene now helps people live on the roof of the world, including in Ladakh and Sikkim.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that useful genes can enter a species by interbreeding and then be favoured by selection.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tibetans breathe thin air with a gift from the Denisovans.

spotlights.name: The Bajau's big spleens
spotlights.spot_it: Sea nomads of Southeast Asia diving with a single breath and wooden goggles to spear fish many metres down.
spotlights.story_md: The **Bajau** have lived on boats and stilt villages in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines for perhaps a thousand years, diving for food. Some reach depths of **70 metres**, and divers can spend more than half their working day underwater. Diving mammals like seals have outsized spleens, which store oxygen-rich red blood cells and squeeze them out during a dive. In **2018** Melissa Ilardo measured Bajau spleens by portable ultrasound and found them about **50% larger** than in their land-farming neighbours, the Saluan, whether or not the individual dived. A gene variant, *PDE10A*, seems to be part of the reason.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A clear case of recent natural selection in humans for a specific way of life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bajau divers carry a seal's trick in their spleen.

spotlights.name: The Rakhigarhi genome
spotlights.spot_it: A grave at India's largest Harappan site, in Haryana, where one skeleton yielded readable ancient DNA.
spotlights.story_md: Hot climates destroy DNA, so the **2019** *Cell* paper led by Vasant Shinde and David Reich was a breakthrough: a genome from a woman buried at **Rakhigarhi** about 4,500 years ago, in the Harappan period. Her ancestry was a mix of ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers and a lineage related to, but separated long before, early farmers and hunter-gatherers of the Iranian plateau. She had **no detectable steppe ancestry**, which appears in South Asia later. Her genetic profile matches part of the ancestry of most people living in India today, making the Harappans one of the main sources of the modern population.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties India's oldest cities to the genes of people living in India now.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Harappan woman's DNA is in most Indians today.

sections.title: What evolution is not
sections.intro_md:
Evolution is taught in Indian schools, debated by politicians and misunderstood almost everywhere. In **January 2018** a minister of state for human resource development said Darwin's theory was 'scientifically wrong' because nobody had seen an ape turn into a human; India's three national science academies issued a joint statement rejecting the claim. Then, as part of a post-pandemic 'rationalisation' of the syllabus announced in 2022, **NCERT** dropped the evolution part of the Class 10 chapter 'Heredity and Evolution'. In **April 2023**, when it became widely known, more than **1,800** scientists and teachers signed an open letter asking for it to be restored.

Most popular confusion comes from a few recurring mistakes:

- 'It is just a theory.' In science a theory is a well-tested explanation, like the germ theory of disease.
- 'Humans came from chimpanzees.' Humans and chimps share an ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago. Neither came from the other.
- 'Evolution has a goal.' It has no direction; it responds to the present.
- 'Survival of the fittest means the strongest win.' Fit means well matched to an environment, measured in offspring.

The spotlights below are four images and ideas that keep these myths alive.

data.Fact: A scientific theory is a tested explanation backed by evidence, like gravity or germs
Humans and chimps share an ancestor from about 6 to 7 million years ago
It has no goal; it follows local conditions
Fittest means best at leaving offspring in that environment
Populations evolve; individuals live and die
Eyes have evolved independently many times, by small steps

spotlights.name: The March of Progress
spotlights.spot_it: A line of figures walking left to right, stooped ape to upright modern man; its ancestor is Huxley's 1863 row of ape skeletons, shown here.
spotlights.story_md: The illustration appeared in the **1965** Time-Life book *Early Man*. It showed **15** primates and humans, and the text explained that many were side branches, not ancestors. But a line of walkers reads as a ladder, and the picture became the world's shorthand for evolution as steady progress towards us. It has been parodied on T-shirts, album covers and protest signs ever since. Scientists dislike it because it shows evolution as a single queue with a destination. The real picture is a bush: many human species, several alive at the same time, most ending in extinction.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single most influential wrong picture of how evolution works.
spotlights.memory_hook: Evolution is a bush, not a parade.

spotlights.name: 'Survival of the fittest'
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian philosopher with large sideburns, the man who coined the phrase Darwin later borrowed.
spotlights.story_md: **Herbert Spencer** coined the phrase in *Principles of Biology* in **1864**, after reading Darwin. Wallace urged Darwin to use it because 'natural selection' sounded like someone doing the selecting, and Darwin added it to the fifth edition of the *Origin* in **1869**. It caused trouble ever since. 'Fit' meant fitting, like a key in a lock, not physically strong. Spencer also applied evolution to society, and others turned that into **social Darwinism**, the claim that poverty and conquest were nature's verdict. Biology says nothing of the kind: a trait's fitness is just how well it gets copied into the next generation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A misread phrase that fed some of the ugliest politics of the last 150 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fit as in a key, not fit as in a gym.

spotlights.name: Trofim Lysenko and the cost of bad biology
spotlights.spot_it: A gaunt Soviet agronomist with intense eyes, often photographed among wheat.
spotlights.story_md: Lysenko rejected genes and natural selection and claimed crops could be trained to new climates and pass the training on, a politically convenient Lamarckism. With **Stalin's** backing, he rose to run Soviet biology. In **1948** genetics was officially condemned and geneticists lost their jobs; some were imprisoned. The great plant geneticist **Nikolai Vavilov**, who had built one of the world's first seed banks, had been arrested in 1940 and died of starvation in prison in **1943**. Lysenko's methods failed in the fields, contributing to poor harvests. Soviet genetics only recovered after he was removed in the mid-1960s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A warning that ideology overruling evidence can cost a country decades of science and food.
spotlights.memory_hook: When politics overruled genes, the wheat did not obey.

spotlights.name: 'If we came from monkeys, why are there still monkeys?'
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian cartoon of Darwin's bearded head on an ape's body, holding a mirror up to another ape.
spotlights.story_md: The question misreads the tree. Humans did not come from chimpanzees or monkeys alive today. We share ancestors with them. Chimps and humans split from a common ancestor roughly **6 to 7 million years** ago; both lines have evolved since. It is like asking: if Americans came from Europeans, why are there still Europeans? Cousins do not replace each other. The 1871 cartoon was a reaction to *The Descent of Man*, where Darwin argued that humans were part of the same tree as other animals. Darwin's own genome-free argument has since been confirmed in detail by DNA.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single most common objection, answered by understanding a family tree.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cousins, not grandparents.

sections.title: What is new, 2024 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
Evolutionary biology is moving faster now than at any time since the 1950s, driven by cheap genome sequencing, ancient DNA and gene editing. In **July 2024** a large study dated LUCA to about 4.2 billion years ago. In **August 2024** Lenski's bacteria passed 80,000 generations, and in **August 2025** the experiment moved back to Michigan State.

The loudest stories came from the company **Colossal Biosciences**, which in 2025 announced gene-edited 'woolly mice' (March) and 'dire wolves' (April), and in 2026 a plan to bring back an extinct African antelope, the bluebuck. Many evolutionary biologists argue that editing a living species to resemble an extinct one does not undo extinction.

Fossils kept arriving too. In **January 2026** researchers published the most complete known skeleton of *Homo habilis*, from Kenya. In **April 2026** came a fossil embryo of *Lystrosaurus*, supporting the view that early mammal relatives laid eggs. In **September 2026** a genomic study named *Leopardus tilcayo*, a small wild cat from Bolivia's Yungas forests, described as the first entirely new living cat species identified in more than a century.

spotlights.name: The 'dire wolves' of 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Fluffy white wolf pups named Romulus, Remus and Khaleesi, and the 13,000-year-old fossils they were modelled on.
spotlights.story_md: Colossal sequenced DNA from a **13,000-year-old tooth** and a **72,000-year-old skull fragment** of the extinct dire wolf. It then made **20 edits in 14 genes** of grey wolf cells to mimic chosen dire wolf traits, such as size and a pale coat, and used dogs as surrogate mothers. Three pups were announced in April 2025. The IUCN's canid specialists said the animals were not dire wolves, and that dire wolves and grey wolves are not even especially close relatives. In May 2025 the company's own chief scientist called them grey wolves with 20 edits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It tests what a species is: a look, a set of genes, or an unbroken lineage of ancestors.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty edits make a white wolf, not a dire one.

spotlights.name: The Harbin skull is a Denisovan
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, heavy-browed human skull with big eye sockets, found by a railway worker in 1933.
spotlights.story_md: The skull was reportedly found in **1933** by a labourer building a bridge in Harbin, northeast China, and hidden in a well for decades. Named *Homo longi*, 'dragon man', in 2021, it is at least **146,000 years** old. In **June 2025**, Qiaomei Fu's team extracted proteins from the skull and mitochondrial DNA from plaque on its one remaining tooth. Both matched the **Denisovans**, known until then mostly from a finger bone, teeth and a jaw. For the first time, scientists may have a face for the people who gave Tibetans their high-altitude gene. Some researchers caution that contamination could affect the DNA result.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives a skull to a human group known mainly from its genes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dragon man has a name now: Denisovan.

sections.title: The whole idea, in one breath
sections.intro_md:
Here is the day in a paragraph. Living things vary, and some of that variation is inherited through DNA. New variation comes from **random mutation**. In each generation, **selection** favours variants that leave more offspring in that environment, **drift** shuffles variants by chance, **gene flow** mixes populations, and **sexual selection** rewards whatever wins mates. Over many generations these forces change populations, and when populations stop interbreeding, they become **new species**.

The evidence comes from many independent directions that all agree: the order of fossils and their transitional forms; the shared, broken and rewired parts of bodies and genomes; the geography of species on islands and continents; and evolution measured directly in finches, moths, lizards, elephants and bacteria.

In **1973** the geneticist Theodosius Dobzhansky gave the subject its most quoted line, the title of his essay: nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution. A virus variant, a resistant infection, a dog breed, a cauliflower, your ability to drink milk and the nerve in your neck all make sense in that light, and in no other.

data.What it does: Creates new variants by DNA copying errors
Favours variants that leave more offspring

spotlights.name: Charles Darwin's last years
spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a long white beard, walking the gravel 'Sandwalk' behind Down House in Kent each day.
spotlights.story_md: Darwin spent his last 40 years at **Down House** in Kent, often ill, doing experiments in his garden and greenhouse. He walked a daily loop he called the **Sandwalk**, his 'thinking path', kicking a flint off the path at each lap to count them. He wrote about orchids, climbing plants, carnivorous plants and emotions. His last book, in **1881**, was about **earthworms**, how they turn soil over and slowly bury old buildings. It sold well. He died on **19 April 1882** and, against his family's wishes for a village burial, was buried in **Westminster Abbey**, a few steps from Isaac Newton.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The patient, experimental life behind the idea is part of why it held up.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who explained life spent his last book on worms.

cards.front: The four forces that change gene frequencies?
